title: Atomic update
description: A single `lock`ed memory operation as a concurrency stepping stone
theory:
### Atomic read-modify-write

Modern CPUs expose **lock-prefixed** instructions that perform an atomic update on a
memory operand visible to other logical processors. For example, **`lock inc qword [mem]`**
reads the quadword, adds one, and writes back without a torn read in the middle—provided
every concurrent writer uses locking or compatible atomics.

This chapter is deliberately small: you see **`lock`** as a prefix on a handful of
instructions, not a full mutex implementation. Real systems combine atomics with **futex**
syscalls, queues, or RCU—but recognizing **`lock`** in disassembly is a prerequisite for
reading low-level performance patches.

### Single-threaded harness, atomic discipline

These exercises still run one thread; the **`lock`** prefix is instructional scaffolding
for how hardware serializes the operation. When you add threads later, every shared
location needs a consistent synchronization strategy—mixing plain loads with locked
updates elsewhere is still a data race in the C11 sense.

```nasm
section .data
    counter: dq 0

section .text
again:
    lock inc qword [rel counter]
    ; ... loop control ...
```

### Where to go next

User-space threads come from **`clone`**-family syscalls and pthreads; kernel schedules
them preemptively. Treat this chapter as connecting **instruction-set atomics** to the
broader concurrency story you will explore in higher-level languages back on top of the
same hardware primitives.

exercises.title: Locked increment
exercises.description: `.data` holds `counter: dq 0`. In a loop of **exactly 5** iterations, execute `lock inc qword [rel counter]`. After the loop, the low byte of `counter` is `5`; print that byte as the character `'5'` (one `write`, no newline), then exit 0.
exercises.starter_code:
global _start
section .data
counter: dq 0
section .bss
    digit: resb 1
section .text
_start:
    mov rcx, 5
again:
    ; lock inc qword [rel counter]
    loop again
    ; materialize '5' into digit and write
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
hints: `lock inc qword [rel counter]` inside the loop
After loop: `movzx eax, byte [rel counter]` then add `'0'` into a byte buffer
exercises.solution:
global _start
section .data
counter: dq 0
section .bss
    digit: resb 1
section .text
_start:
    mov rcx, 5
again:
    lock inc qword [rel counter]
    loop again
    movzx eax, byte [rel counter]
    add eax, '0'
    mov [rel digit], al
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel digit]
    mov rdx, 1
    syscall
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall

exercises.title: Decrement to zero
exercises.description: Start `counter: dq 3`. Loop until it becomes `0` using `lock dec qword [rel counter]` each iteration (three iterations). The numeric value is now `0`; print the **character** `'0'` (ASCII 0x30) by writing one byte (for example load the byte at `counter`, add `'0'`, store to a scratch byte, then `write`), then exit 0.
exercises.starter_code:
global _start
section .data
counter: dq 3
section .bss
    out: resb 1
section .text
_start:
    ; loop: lock dec; jnz
    ; then emit ASCII '0'
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
hints: Compare `qword [rel counter]` against 0 with `cmp qword [rel counter], 0` / `jnz`
exercises.solution:
global _start
section .data
counter: dq 3
section .bss
    out: resb 1
section .text
_start:
again:
    lock dec qword [rel counter]
    cmp qword [rel counter], 0
    jnz again
    movzx eax, byte [rel counter]
    add eax, '0'
    mov [rel out], al
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel out]
    mov rdx, 1
    syscall
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall

exercises.title: XADD exchange
exercises.description: Memory `value` starts at `0`. `mov rax, 7` then `lock xadd qword [rel value], rax` adds into memory and leaves the **old** memory value in `rax` (here `0`). Memory becomes `7`. Print the character `'7'` by taking the low byte of `value`, adding `'0'`, writing one byte (reuse a `.bss` scratch byte if you like), then exit 0.
exercises.starter_code:
global _start
section .data
value: dq 0
section .bss
    digit: resb 1
section .text
_start:
    mov rax, 7
    ; lock xadd qword [rel value], rax
    ; print digit from memory at value
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
hints: After `xadd`, load a byte from `value` and turn it into ASCII with `add reg, '0'`
exercises.solution:
global _start
section .data
value: dq 0
section .bss
    digit: resb 1
section .text
_start:
    mov rax, 7
    lock xadd qword [rel value], rax
    movzx eax, byte [rel value]
    add eax, '0'
    mov [rel digit], al
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel digit]
    mov rdx, 1
    syscall
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall

exercises.title: Locked add immediate
exercises.description: Memory `v: dq 2`. Execute **`lock add qword [rel v], 5`**. The sum is `7`. Print the character `'7'` with a one-byte `write` (materialize via a `.bss` scratch byte like earlier exercises), then exit 0.
exercises.starter_code:
global _start
section .data
v: dq 2
section .bss
    digit: resb 1
section .text
_start:
    ; lock add qword [rel v], 5
    ; print digit for low byte of v (value 7 -> '7')
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
exercises.solution:
global _start
section .data
v: dq 2
section .bss
    digit: resb 1
section .text
_start:
    lock add qword [rel v], 5
    movzx eax, byte [rel v]
    add eax, '0'
    mov [rel digit], al
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel digit]
    mov rdx, 1
    syscall
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
